questions.q: In the Q# Teleport operation, what are m1 and m2, and how are they used?
options: They are qubits that get entangled with the receiver
They are classical Result values from measuring the sender's two qubits, used in ordinary if-conditioned X/Z corrections applied to the receiver's qubit
They are randomly generated angles used to rotate the receiver's qubit
They are unused debug variables with no effect on the protocol
questions.explain: m1 and m2 are the two classical measurement outcomes from the sender's qubits; the receiver's correction (X if m2==One, Z if m1==One) is ordinary classical control flow on these Result values.

questions.q: What happens to the original qubit (msg) during teleportation?
options: It is copied, so both msg and there end up in the same state
It is measured and destroyed in the process -- teleportation moves the state, it does not clone it, consistent with the no-cloning theorem
It remains completely unaffected and reusable afterward
It is physically transported to the receiver's location
questions.explain: Teleportation necessarily consumes the original qubit via measurement; no physical qubit travels and no copy is made, consistent with the no-cloning theorem.

questions.q: For the verified example (teleporting |+>), what was the exact probability of each of the 4 possible (m1, m2) measurement outcomes?
options: Exactly 0.25 for each of the 4 outcomes, confirmed by direct matrix computation of the full 3-qubit state
1.0 for one outcome and 0 for the other three
0.5 for two outcomes and 0 for the other two
The probabilities could not be determined without running real hardware
questions.explain: Building the 3-qubit state explicitly and applying the CNOT+H Bell-basis change confirmed each of the 4 (m1,m2) outcomes occurs with probability exactly 0.25.

questions.q: After applying the correction indicated by whichever (m1, m2) outcome occurred, what was the verified fidelity between the receiver's final state and the original |+> state?
options: Exactly 1.0 -- the receiver's corrected qubit exactly reproduces the original state, not an approximation
Approximately 0.95, due to unavoidable protocol noise
Exactly 0.25, matching the measurement outcome probability
0, since teleportation destroys the original information permanently
questions.explain: Applying the outcome-appropriate Pauli correction (X and/or Z as needed) was verified to exactly reproduce the original |+> state in every case -- fidelity 1.0, not approximate.

questions.q: Why does teleportation NOT allow faster-than-light communication, according to the lesson's reasoning?
options: Because entanglement does not actually exist

Because the receiver's qubit alone, without the classical bits m1/m2, is indistinguishable regardless of what the sender measured -- the actual information (which correction to apply) only travels via the classical bits, which cannot exceed light speed
Because teleportation only works over short distances
Because the protocol requires the sender and receiver to already be in the same location
questions.explain: Without the classically-transmitted m1/m2 bits, the receiver's qubit looks the same no matter what happened at the sender's end -- the useful information transfer is bottlenecked by the classical channel, which respects the speed-of-light limit.
